doc.title: Frank Alkyer interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Orleans, Louisiana, January 10, 2020

chapter: Writing about jazz and reviewing records
title: Reviewing EPs, singles and streaming; how artists get records reviewed
summary: DownBeat will treat EPs and singles like 78 sides. It gets about 50,000 records a year and reviews 500-600, so artists must follow up.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Have you started down the path of reviewing musical releases that are not a physical product?

Yeah. I don’t think that there’s any way around that. It’s like that has changed. We were talking the other day about, because now there’s a trend that’s coming up that people are not releasing full albums, they’re releasing an EP, an extended play record of maybe four songs, or even singles. And how is DownBeat going to handle that? And I look at it and I go, I think we’ll handle it exactly how we did back when we first started doing reviews in the era of the 78, when there were just two sides. So you would review the two sides of that record and that was it. There was no album. It was just a 78 and it would have two songs, one on each side, and I go we’re just going full circle.
So the hopeful musician, they pay for the recording themselves, they make their own CDs and they put it in an envelope and they send it to DownBeat. Is that fruitless?

No it’s not. It’s not fruitless. But we get about 50,000 records a year. We, in the magazine itself maybe we review five to six hundred. So you know maybe ten to fifteen percent of the records that we get in. But even in sending it to us a lot of people just email it to us. We get links now. We get them digitally, and a lot of times we’re not even getting the physical product. We still do. Those things come in, and you know I’ve got bins in my office and the reviews editor has three times as many bins in his office. But a lot of times we get them in but what has to happen is the artist, you’ve got to follow up. If you send it out into the ether, you need to have somebody that’s going to follow up and call us and say, “Hey did you get this? Did it arrive?” All those things. Because there are 50,000

pieces of music that come into the office every year. And during certain periods it’s much busier than others. So you’ve got to make a phone call and try to get that to the top of the list for us to give it a listen to see if we’re going to review it or not.
